pick.headline: Car bomb targeting Fadlallah kills dozens in Beirut
pick.summary: On March 8, 1985, a car bomb exploded near the Beirut home of Shi'a cleric Muhammad Husayn Fadlallah, who survived; about eighty people were killed.
pick.significance: The bombing was later linked by the press to a Lebanese unit trained with CIA support, an allegation the agency denied. It deepened Shi'a hostility to the United States.
pick.fbis: The South Asia Daily Report of March 11, 1985, carried a review citing Beirut radio that the March 8 car bomb near Shaykh Fadlallah's home in Bi'r al-'Abd killed 72 and wounded 255; Fadlallah blamed "Israel and its local allies", which Israel's cabinet denied.

evidence.title: FBIS Daily Report: South Asia, Vol. VIII No. 047, 11 March 1985
evidence.snippet: …8 March car-bomb in the Bi‘r al-‘Abd area of southern Beirut — an explosion which killed 72 people and wounded 255, according to Beirut radio That bomb went off near the home of Shi‘ite theologian Shaykh Muhammad Husayn Fadlallah, who subsequently accused “Israel and its local allies” of the attack in remarks broadcast by the clandestine Voice of the Mountain radio. alternates.headline: Reagan calls the USSR an 'evil empire'
alternates.summary: On March 8, 1983, President Reagan described the Soviet Union as an 'evil empire' in a speech to evangelicals in Orlando, Florida.
alternates.significance: The speech crystallized the confrontational rhetoric of the early 1980s and drew furious Soviet responses.
alternates.fbis: The Soviet Union Daily Report of March 10, 1983, carried Moscow TASS calling Reagan's Orlando speech to evangelicals "another of his provocative speeches" of "lunatic anticommunism" and extreme militarism, right after a KGB announcement expelling U.S. diplomat Richard Osborn for espionage.
